I've been fiddling around with meltano and finicky singer taps for 2 weeks, and today I found dlt. What a breath of fresh air -- thank you for the work! I think this is the future over the meltano and singer ecosystem -- the code quality, simplicity and ease of integration into my project, and documentation really makes this project shine.

We are one of the early adopters and really like the 'weight' of DLT. It's heavy enough to be adding substantial value over homegrown scripts for extraction and loading. At the same time, it is light enough to be easy to add to a pre-existing data stack.

This is nice. Pulling data from an API and putting it in a SQL database should be a simple everyday task but the tools for this are 99% massive overkill. Great to see a simple library for a simple job.
Nicely done! Looks lightweight and powerful - especially the schema auto-generation and flattening will make many raw data tables look much cleaner.

Automatic schema evolution is criticized as an anti-feature by a commenter: 'This is the opposite of what I want in 99% of projects... A schema essentially forms a business-critical contract between two major sections of the overall data pipeline, and that is absolutely not something I want to be changing dynamically without my explicit understanding and consent.'
As an FYI, Databricks' 'Delta Live Tables' product keeps being contracted to 'DLT' at my employer, so you have some potential naming confusion in your future.
Tbh I found it confusing why suddenly you were using chatgpt in the middle of the example. It made it seem like this is a gpt based tool but it's not.

Skimming over the demo, I couldn't tell where your library actually got involved at all, it just looked like a couple of functions to access data, followed by links to your documentation. I suggest dumping the whole thing and starting with a more coherent demo that focuses on the features of the tool you actually built.

A commenter noted a practical infra gap: dltHub responded 'We took at least one immediate practical good piece of advice out of this which is that we should release a conda package and make sure that dlt works in it.'

dltHub Show HN launch of dlt-init-openapi: 'Now dlt helps its users to code around a thousand new data sources each month and to maintain many thousands of live datasets in production.' A core contributor called the new OpenAPI toolkit 'wonderful and will greatly simplify the life of everybody dealing with small APIs that follow the OpenAPI standards.'

One of the reasons why I like dlt is because I can do everything via code, which makes things more maintainable, for me. I think this could be a starting point for a dlt SaaS, but there are a lot of things to consider and connectors change all the time.
